item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating persistent preferences from immediate intent. [MSMT-LSI (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s44196-024-00460-5) combines multitemporal embeddings with separate long-/short-term attention; its evaluation notes weaker performance on sparse Amazon histories, where temporal evidence is limited. [LS4SRec (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3723173) uses independent interest encoders plus a global interaction graph to supply collaborative signals under sparsity. [Dual-frequency self-attention (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2025.122700) explicitly separates low-/high-frequency preference information and adds contrastive learning. These approaches motivate multiple interest timescales, but do not establish gains on the pinned four-category benchmark.\n\nA practical architecture hypothesis: retain SASRec for sequential context, add a recent-window intent encoder and a pooled persistent-interest encoder, then learn a fusion gate conditioned on history length, timestamp gaps and agreement between branches. Timestamp decay should be learned or bucketed; aggressive fixed decay could discard useful evidence in sparse histories. [GDA-REIM (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2026.108721) combines gated attention denoising with separate repetition/exploration scoring, suggesting that noise suppression and intent separation can reinforce each other. However, exact-item repetition scoring has limited relevance when recommendations exclude previously seen items; transfer the idea to recurring patterns among unseen candidates. This proposed adaptation is an inference from the literature, requiring controlled ablations of recent pooling, long-term pooling, gating and temporal features using macro validation HR@10."}
